title: Inorganic Chemistry
lines: Inorganic questions in USAT test the periodic table and its trends, the chemistry of the s, p and d blocks, and the main industrial processes. Most are recall questions: a trend and its exception, a formula, a colour, a catalyst or the condition used in a process. Learn the reasons behind the trends, because questions often ask why.
## The periodic table
- The modern table is arranged by atomic number (Moseley), not atomic mass (Mendeleev). It has 7 periods and 18 groups.
- Period lengths: 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32. The period number is the highest shell in use.
- s block: groups 1-2 (ns¹⁻²). p block: groups 13-18 (ns² np¹⁻⁶). d block: groups 3-12. f block: lanthanides and actinides.
> Example 1. An element has Z = 35. Find its configuration, period, group and block.
> [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵: highest shell n = 4, so period 4; seven outer electrons in s and p, so group 17 in the p block. It is bromine.
## Periodic trends
| Property | Across a period | Down a group
| Atomic radius | decreases | increases
| Ionisation energy | increases | decreases
| Electronegativity | increases | decreases
| Metallic character | decreases | increases
- Across a period the nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell, so they are pulled in more tightly. Down a group new shells are added and inner electrons shield the outer ones.
- Ionisation energy dips: Be > B and Mg > Al (a p electron is easier to remove than an s² electron); N > O and P > S (half-filled p³ is extra stable).
- Chlorine has a higher electron affinity than fluorine because the small fluorine atom crowds the incoming electron.
- Cations are smaller than their atoms; anions are larger. In an isoelectronic series, more protons mean a smaller ion.
> Example 2. Arrange O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Al³⁺ in order of decreasing size.
> All have 10 electrons; the nuclear charge rises from 8 to 13. So O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺.
- Period 3 oxides change from basic (Na₂O, MgO) through amphoteric (Al₂O₃) to acidic (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇).
## The s block
- Group 1 (alkali metals) and group 2 (alkaline earth metals) are reactive metals; reactivity rises down each group as ionisation energy falls.
- Flame colours: Li crimson, Na golden yellow, K lilac, Ca brick red, Sr crimson red, Ba apple green.
- Down group 2, hydroxides become more soluble and sulphates less soluble (BaSO₄ is insoluble). Carbonates become more stable to heat.
- Lithium resembles magnesium, and beryllium resembles aluminium (diagonal relationship). BeO is amphoteric.
- Compounds to know: NaOH from the electrolysis of brine; Na₂CO₃ by the Solvay process; quicklime CaO from heating limestone; slaked lime Ca(OH)₂; gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O and plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O.
## The p block
- Boron and aluminium (group 13): borax Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O; boric acid H₃BO₃ is a weak Lewis acid. Al₂O₃ and Al(OH)₃ are amphoteric. Alum purifies water by coagulating suspended particles.
- Group 14: catenation is strongest for carbon. Down the group the +2 state becomes more stable (inert pair effect), so Pb²⁺ is the stable lead ion and PbO₂ is an oxidising agent.
- Nitrogen and phosphorus (group 15): N₂ is unreactive because of its strong triple bond. White phosphorus is very reactive and stored under water; red phosphorus is far more stable.
- Oxygen and sulphur (group 16): ozone O₃ in the stratosphere absorbs ultraviolet. Concentrated H₂SO₄ is a dehydrating agent (it chars sugar) and an oxidising agent.
- Halogens (group 17): oxidising power F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂, so chlorine displaces bromine and iodine from their salts. With silver nitrate, Cl⁻ gives a white precipitate, Br⁻ cream and I⁻ yellow.
- Noble gases (group 18) are very unreactive, but xenon forms fluorides such as XeF₂, XeF₄ and XeF₆.
## The d block (transition elements)
- Electrons enter the (n − 1)d subshell; on forming ions the 4s electrons are lost first.

- Typical properties: variable oxidation states (Mn reaches +7 in KMnO₄), coloured ions (due to d-d transitions), paramagnetism from unpaired electrons, complex formation and catalytic activity (Fe in Haber, V₂O₅ in the contact process, Ni in hydrogenation).
- Ions with d⁰ or d¹⁰ configurations (Sc³⁺, Zn²⁺) are colourless. Zinc is not a typical transition element.
- Magnetic moment (spin only) = √(n(n + 2)) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons.
- In acid, purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to almost colourless Mn²⁺ (gaining 5 electrons) and orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ to green Cr³⁺ (6 electrons per ion).
> Example 3. Find the number of unpaired electrons and the spin-only magnetic moment of Fe³⁺ (Z = 26).
> Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²; Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵ with 5 unpaired electrons. μ = √(5 × 7) = √35 ≈ 5.9 BM.
## Industrial chemistry
| Process | Reaction | Catalyst, conditions
| Haber (ammonia) | N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ | iron; about 450 °C, about 200 atm
| Contact (sulphuric acid) | 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ | V₂O₅; about 450 °C, 1-2 atm
| Ostwald (nitric acid) | 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O | platinum-rhodium gauze
- Both Haber and contact reactions are exothermic, so a moderate temperature is a compromise between yield and rate.
- In the contact process SO₃ is absorbed in 98 % H₂SO₄ to give oleum, which is then diluted; SO₃ added straight to water forms a fine acid mist.
- Urea CO(NH₂)₂ is made from ammonia and carbon dioxide and contains about 46.7 % nitrogen, more than any other common solid fertiliser.
- Portland cement is made by heating limestone with clay; a little gypsum is added to slow the setting.
- Acid rain comes mainly from SO₂ and oxides of nitrogen; CFCs destroy stratospheric ozone.
> Example 4. Find the percentage of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃ (N = 14, H = 1, O = 16).
! Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶, not [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s²: the 4s electrons leave first.
! The strongest bond among the halogens is Cl-Cl, not F-F, yet fluorine is still the strongest oxidising agent.
! A catalyst in the Haber process does not raise the yield of ammonia; it only gets to equilibrium faster.
## Quick check
- Element with the highest electronegativity? (fluorine)
- Flame colour of potassium? (lilac)
- Catalyst in the contact process? (vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅)
- Why is Zn²⁺ colourless? (3d¹⁰: no d-d transitions)
- Which has the larger first ionisation energy, N or O? (N)
